title: 7. Four-Gate (四門) Hwajaeng and the Four Modes of Correlative Thinking
content:
The four modes of correlative thinking examined in Part I—multidimensionality (立體), circulation (循環), empathy (共感), and convergence (融合)—form a remarkable structural correspondence with the historical unfolding of Buddhist *hwajaeng* thought. The *hwajaeng* (和諍) thought of Wonhyo (元曉, 617–686) begins from a binary (二項) opposition and expands into ternary (三項) and quaternary (四項) relations, showing at each stage a philosophical structure that corresponds exactly to the laws of correlative thinking in Part I (Kim Sang-il, 2003).

### 7.1. The Starting Point of Binary (二項) Hwajaeng: The Gate of Suchness (Madhyamaka) and the Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing (Consciousness-Only) → Linkage with Multidimensional Thinking (Mimesis)

The binary means a structure of two standing face to face. The Gate of Suchness (眞如門) can be understood as pointing to the dimension of essence, and the Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing (生滅門) to the dimension of change. Simply put, one sees the deep ground, the other sees the movement that appears before the eyes.

Translated into a student's daily life, it resembles the relationship between school rules and the actual classroom scene. Seeing only the rules, one sees the principle but not the complexity of reality; seeing only the actual scene, one easily loses direction. The Gate of Suchness and the Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing make one see these two dimensions together.

This is also why binary *hwajaeng* is linked to multidimensional thinking. For when two different perspectives are erected at once, the depth of reality becomes visible.

In the system of the *Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith* (大乘起信論), the starting point of Wonhyo's *hwajaeng* is the binary (二項) relation of the Gate of Suchness (眞如門) and the Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing (生滅門). The Gate of Suchness, as the essence of mind, treats the aspect of "empty, tranquil, numinous awareness" (空寂靈知) and corresponds to Madhyamaka (中觀) thought. The Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing treats the change of the phenomenal world and the operation centered on the *ālaya-vijñāna* (阿賴耶識) and corresponds to Consciousness-Only (唯識) thought.

Master Wonhyo integrated these as "one mind, two gates" (一心二門). If the Gate of Suchness is essence (體)—the essential aspect—then the Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing is function (用)—the phenomenal operation.

Linkage with the multidimensional thinking (Mimesis) of Part I, Chapter 2: the binary *hwajaeng* of the Gate of Suchness and the Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing corresponds exactly to the logical structure of Daoist mimesis. The emptiness (空) of Madhyamaka and the consciousness (識) of Consciousness-Only, while negating each other, are subsumed as one within the one mind (一心).

### 7.2. The Deepening of Ternary (三項) Hwajaeng: The Three Natures Doctrine of Consciousness-Only (三性說) → Linkage with Circular Thinking (Mythos)

The ternary is a structure in which one more mediator has entered between the two. It resembles how, when two friends quarrel, the entry of a third perspective makes the structure of the fight newly visible. With only two, it is a fight of right/wrong; but when a third perspective enters, the relationship begins to move.

The Three Natures doctrine does not fix the world at once but distinguishes the layer of discrimination, the layer of relationship, and the layer of completion. So it functions like a staircase on which thought matures one step at a time.

In this respect, ternary *hwajaeng* connects well with circular thinking. For a movement occurs that goes back and forth between the two extremes and advances toward a deeper understanding.

The developed Three Natures doctrine (三性說) of Consciousness-Only thought is a refined philosophical tool that expands the existing binary *hwajaeng* of Madhyamaka and Consciousness-Only into a ternary (三項) relation. The Three Natures consist of the imagined nature (遍計所執性), the dependent nature (依他起性), and the perfected nature (圓成實性).

The core insight of the Three Natures doctrine is the proposition: "If, upon the dependent nature, you remove the imagined nature, that itself is the perfected nature."

The following table presents the binary relation of the Gate of Suchness and the Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing and its conversion into a ternary relation.

**Table 7.1 The Binary Relation of the Gate of Suchness and the Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing**

| Category | Gate of Suchness (眞如門) | Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing (生滅門) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Philosophical stance | Essence (體) — the essential aspect | Function (用) — the phenomenal operation |
| Principal school | Madhyamaka (中觀) | Consciousness-Only (唯識) |
| Core concept | Refuting error (破邪) — shattering mistaken views | Manifesting the right (顯正) — revealing correct principle |
| Character | Absolute equality (being empty) | Relative differentiation (following conditions) |

**Table 7.2 Conversion of the Gate of Suchness and the Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing into a Ternary Relation**

| Existing two-fold hwajaeng (Awakening of Faith) | Expanded hwajaeng based on the Three Natures of Consciousness-Only | The logic of hwajaeng |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gate of Suchness (眞如) | Perfected nature (圓成實性) | Absolute truth (full even while empty) |
| Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing (生滅) | Dependent nature (依他起性) | Phenomenal dependent arising (manifestation according to conditions) |
| (Subordinate to the Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing) | Imagined nature (遍計所執性) | Subjective delusion (the object to be shattered) |

Examining the linkage with the circular thinking (Mythos) of Part I, Chapter 3 [3]: the ternary *hwajaeng* structure of the Three Natures doctrine corresponds to the logic of Buddhist mythos. The dependent nature circularly mediates between the imagined nature and the perfected nature, simultaneously overcoming nihilism and substantialism.

### 7.3. The Completion of Quaternary (四項) Hwajaeng: The Addition of the Pure Land Gate (淨土門) and the Four-Gate Oppositional Structure → Linkage with Empathic Thinking (Logos)

The quaternary structure is a thinking that sees four directions together. It is like a map that sees not only front and back but east, west, south, and north together. With the addition of the Pure Land Gate, *hwajaeng* comes to embrace, beyond a mere analytic system, even the sense of salvation on which the human can actually rely and live.

The following table shows the conversion of *hwajaeng*, fused with the Pure Land Gate, into a quaternary relation.

**Table 8: Conversion of Hwajaeng, Fused with the Pure Land Gate, into a Quaternary Relation**

| Name | Core character | Seasonal assignment | The role of hwajaeng |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gate of Suchness (眞如門) | Absolute emptying (Madhyamaka) | Autumn | Return to essence (refuting phenomena) |
| Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing (生滅門) | The arising of phenomena (Awakening of Faith) | Spring | Understanding of phenomena (representation) |
| Gate of the Three Natures (三性門) | Analysis of being (Consciousness-Only) | Summer | Discernment of the false from the true |
| Pure Land Gate (淨土門) | The salvation of compassion (Pure Land school) | Winter | Practical refuge and rest |

What matters is that the four gates are not separate rooms warring with one another. Each is a different gate by which the human understands the world, and through whichever gate one enters, one meets, in the end, within the same larger house.

The connection with empathic thinking is revealed here too. For empathy is not merely imitating the other but the attitude of acknowledging that, outside the gate I entered, other gates also exist.

To set Pure Land Buddhism (淨土宗) as one independent gate (門) and thereby expand the structure of *hwajaeng* into four gates (四門) is a highly valid attempt to reinterpret Master Wonhyo's thought in a modern way. The oppositional structure of the four gates consists of two axes facing each other. Vertical opposition: the Gate of Suchness and the Pure Land Gate face each other. Horizontal opposition: the Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing and the Gate of the Three Natures face each other. Wonhyo resolves this with the logic of opening-and-merging (開合)—unfolded, they are four; merged, they are one.

### 7.4. Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter: The Circulation of the Four Gates and Hwajaeng → Linkage with Convergent Thinking

The analogy of the four seasons makes *hwajaeng* easiest to understand. Just as one cannot say that spring alone is a good season and winter is useless, the four gates of thought each take on a different role. There must be the functions of beginning, growth, reflection, and storage for the whole of life to continue.

Our society easily clings to and lives by one particular season. For example, if growth and speed alone are emphasized, society becomes one in which summer alone continues, and as a result people grow exhausted and the community dries up. *Hwajaeng* makes us ask, "In which season is our society now confined?"

Convergent thinking reads these four seasons as a single great rhythm. When we understand that the different stages do not collide but turn in sequence, conflict becomes a problem not of destruction but of rearrangement. The following table shows the relation between spring-summer-autumn-winter and the four-gate *hwajaeng*.

**Table 9: The Relation between Spring-Summer-Autumn-Winter and the Four-Gate Hwajaeng**

| Season | Gate (門) | Related thought | The core of hwajaeng |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spring | Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing | Huayan | Just as the universe is contained in a single flower (one is many), the arising-and-ceasing phenomenon is itself truth |
| Summer | Gate of the Three Natures | Seon (Zen) | The intensity of cutting delusion (the imagined) at a single stroke to intuit the essence (the perfected) |
| Autumn | Gate of Suchness | *Tathāgatagarbha* | Stripping off all husks to confirm the pure seed of buddhahood within |
| Winter | Pure Land Gate | Pure Land | Holding the seed and resting in the vast bosom of compassion, preparing new life |

The four-gate (四門) *hwajaeng*, when arranged in the circular order of spring-summer-autumn-winter, makes its dynamic meaning all the more vivid.

- **[Spring (春) — Gate of Arising-and-Ceasing]** The beginning of life, in which all dharmas sprout according to conditions from the *ālaya-vijñāna*. "When mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise (心生卽種種法生)."
- **[Summer (夏) — Gate of the Three Natures]** The period of intense practice following the law of conditions (the dependent nature), discerning the fruit (the perfected) from the weeds (the imagined).
- **[Autumn (秋) — Gate of Suchness]** The quiet, convergent stage of laying down all phenomena (arising-and-ceasing) and discrimination (the three natures) and returning to the empty essence, emptiness (空).
- **[Winter (冬) — Pure Land Gate]** The rest and vow of admitting that one's own power is exhausted, and, sinking completely into the original power of Amitābha, preparing to be reborn.

The arising of spring (arising-and-ceasing) faces the vanishing of autumn (suchness), and the intense analysis of summer (three natures) faces the unconditional acceptance of winter (Pure Land).

### 7.5. The Grand Integration of *Tathāgatagarbha*, Pure Land, Huayan, and Seon: The Philosophy of Affirmation and Hwajaeng

This section is difficult because of its many names, but its core is one: that different traditions are, in the end, using different languages to understand the possibility within the human and the affirmativeness of the world.

Some traditions emphasize the original brightness; some emphasize the world of salvation; and yet others emphasize a vast web of relationship in which all things are connected to one another. Though the expressions differ, together they say that the human is not a being thrown only toward despair.

*Hwajaeng* is precisely the work of reading this common ground. It is the philosophy that reveals that different names do not mean complete severance, and that even within difference there is a connecting center.

*Tathāgatagarbha* (如來藏), Pure Land (淨土), Huayan (華嚴), and Seon (禪宗) share the dazzling world of affirmation reached at the end of the analysis of Madhyamaka and Consciousness-Only. The greatest commonality of these four thoughts is the logic of original enlightenment (本覺, being originally enlightened).

*Tathāgatagarbha* and Pure Land are like two sides of a coin. Wonhyo, while saying "the Pure Land is the pure mind (*tathāgatagarbha*) itself," did not in fact deny an actual Western Pure Land. The reason they meet is that they share the logic of *hwajaeng*: from negation to affirmation, the unity of self-power and other-power, and the dissolution of the boundary between the ordinary person and the sage.
